queue.title: Gully erosion threatens homes, farmlands in Gombe community
queue.description: Residents of Kumo, headquarters of Akko Local Government Area of Gombe State, have raised the alarm over the worsening gully erosion threatening homes, farmlands and roads in several parts of the town. The residents, particularly those in Zadawa, Jauro Musa, Nasarawo and Waziri Malle communities, said the erosion had continued to expand, destroying portions of […]
queue.content:
Residents of Kumo, headquarters of Akko Local Government Area of Gombe State, have raised the alarm over the worsening gully erosion threatening homes, farmlands and roads in several parts of the town.

The residents, particularly those in Zadawa, Jauro Musa, Nasarawo and Waziri Malle communities, said the erosion had continued to expand, destroying portions of farmland and encroaching on residential areas.

According to them, some houses have already been affected, while several others are at risk of collapse if urgent intervention is not provided.

A community development advocate, Bello Barambu, appealed to the Gombe State Government, Akko Local Government Council and relevant federal agencies to urgently intervene to prevent further destruction.

Barambu called for the deployment of environmental and engineering experts to assess the extent of the damage and recommend lasting solutions, including the construction and rehabilitation of drainage channels and measures to control the expansion of the gullies.

He also appealed to the Agro-Climatic Resilience in Semi-Arid Landscapes (ACReSAL), the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) and the Gombe State Emergency Management Agency (SEMA) to collaborate in providing relief and intervention to affected residents.

“This is not just a complaint; it is a cry for help. We need intervention now before the situation turns into a major disaster,” Barambu said.

The residents further appealed to their representatives in the legislature, development organisations and other stakeholders to support efforts to protect lives, homes and livelihoods from the growing threat.

queue.title: N’Assembly has over 14,000 workers, busiest parliament in world — Clerk
queue.description: The National Assembly has more than 14,000 workers, excluding 469 federal lawmakers and their visitors, making it the busiest parliament in the world, the Clerk to the National Assembly (CNA), Kamoru Ogunlana, has said. Ogunlana spoke on Tuesday at the final phase of a capacity-building programme for legislative aides in the 10th National Assembly. He […]
queue.content:
The National Assembly has more than 14,000 workers, excluding 469 federal lawmakers and their visitors, making it the busiest parliament in the world, the Clerk to the National Assembly (CNA), Kamoru Ogunlana, has said.
Ogunlana spoke on Tuesday at the final phase of a capacity-building programme for legislative aides in the 10th National Assembly.
He said the large workforce, lawmakers and daily visitors made the administration of the federal parliament particularly demanding.
“No parliament in the world is as busy as the National Assembly, which has over 14,000 personnel aside from the federal legislators and their visitors,” he said.
Ogunlana also said the Senate and House of Representatives had passed 3,500 bills in the last three years.
He said the Senate passed 1,500 bills, while the House passed 2,000.
According to him, the volume of legislative activities underscores the need for an efficient support system for lawmakers.
The clerk renewed his call for a special salary structure for legislative aides, describing them as an important part of the legislative process.
He urged the National Assembly Service Commission (NASC) and the Revenue Mobilisation Allocation and Fiscal Commission (RMAFC) to resolve issues relating to the salaries and conditions of service of the aides.
“There is a need to streamline the responsibility of the NASC and RMAFC in determining the salaries and conditions of service of legislative aides,” he said.
Ogunlana said that while NASC handles the appointment and administration of legislative aides, their remuneration operates within a framework developed or approved by RMAFC and subject to National Assembly approval.
He said the appointments were temporary and non-pensionable, urging reforms to improve their welfare and strengthen their capacity to support lawmakers.

queue.title: Despite peace deal, banditry persists across Katsina communities
queue.description: Months after local governments, community leaders and other stakeholders brokered peace agreements with bandit groups in parts of Katsina State, residents said the deals had failed to end killings, abductions, livestock rustling and displacement. The scale of the crisis is reflected in the number of people forced from their homes. Data from the International Organisation […]
queue.content:
Months after local governments, community leaders and other stakeholders brokered peace agreements with bandit groups in parts of Katsina State, residents said the deals had failed to end killings, abductions, livestock rustling and displacement.

The scale of the crisis is reflected in the number of people forced from their homes. Data from the International Organisation for Migration (IOM) showed that more than 138,000 people were displaced by insecurity and natural disasters in Katsina between January 2025 and January 2026.

In a bid to end the violence and enable residents to return to their farms, several communities entered into agreements with armed groups. Under the arrangements, the bandits were expected to stop attacks, release kidnapped victims and allow residents to carry out their daily activities.

The agreements also allowed the bandits access to communities, including markets and health facilities.

The Katsina State Government, however, said the peace initiatives were driven by affected communities and not by the state.

Despite the agreements, residents in Bakori, Malumfashi, Dutsinma, Matazu, Musawa, Faskari, Dandume, Kankia and other areas told Daily Trust that bandits continued to operate.

In Bakori, where a peace agreement was reached at Kakumi several months ago, residents said there had been little improvement.

A former chairman of Bakori Local Government Council and resident of Shuwaki, Aminu Magaji, said about 200 people were in the hands of bandits following repeated abductions.

He said hundreds of residents had also been displaced and many had lost their means of livelihood.

“Since the peace deal, there has never been a week without an attack by bandits,” Magaji said.

Another resident of Guga community, Mahadi Dan Binta Guga, said the peace process was flawed, alleging a lack of commitment and adequate security measures.

He called for the deployment of security personnel to affected communities and urged the authorities to dislodge the bandits from their enclaves.

In Malumfashi, residents said the agreement had also failed to halt attacks.

Naziru Mu’azu, a resident of Gidan Mantau, where dozens of people were killed in a mosque in a previous attack, said residents were still living in fear.

“Despite the initial peace deal, the bandits are still attacking our communities. People are still living in fear,” he said.

Ibrahim Galadima, a resident of Gidan Mai Jimina in eastern Malumfashi, said the agreement had weakened local vigilantes who previously confronted attackers.

He said vigilantes were reluctant to respond to attacks for fear of being accused of violating the agreement.

“The peace deal only succeeded in exposing us more. Our vigilantes cannot respond when bandits attack because if they do, they are accused of violating the peace deal,” Galadima said.

Two local government chairmen, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the agreements needed to be regularly reviewed and renewed.

They cited Jibia and Batsari as examples where similar arrangements had, at certain periods, brought relief to residents. However, they stressed that dialogue must be backed by stronger security measures.

In Dutsinma, prolonged insecurity has forced many residents to flee their communities. Some displaced persons are reportedly living in uncompleted buildings and public places in Baggagadi, Kuki and other towns.

The displacement has also cut families off from their farms, livestock and other sources of livelihood.

Residents of Matazu and Musawa also reported attacks, abductions and livestock rustling, particularly in rural communities near forest areas.

Similar challenges persist in Faskari and Dandume, where insecurity has disrupted farming and livestock production.

Kankia has also recorded fresh attacks. Residents said 13 people were killed in Unguwar Guru and Walawa communities in Sukuntuni Ward in attacks allegedly carried out by fighters loyal to a notorious bandit leader identified as Kachalla Maha.

Seven people were reportedly killed in Unguwar Guru last weekend before the attackers returned on Monday, August 17, killing more people and extending the assault to Walawa.

Several women and girls were also reportedly abducted, while houses and shops were set ablaze.

Bakori also recorded fresh violence, with suspected bandits killing three people, including two children and an elderly man, in Gidan Bawa, Kandarawa Ward.

About eight people, mostly women, were reportedly abducted, while livestock were rustled.

Relative calm in Jibia, Batsari, Safana, Danmusa

However, the peace initiatives have yielded some results in parts of the state.

Jibia, Batsari, Safana and Danmusa, as well as some parts of Dutsinma, have recorded periods of relative calm, allowing residents to gradually return to farming and other economic activities.

The chairman of Jibia LGA, Alhaji Surajo Ado, said the initiative had recorded significant successes despite recent setbacks.

He acknowledged reports of killings, injuries and livestock rustling, particularly in eastern Jibia, but said the overall security situation had improved.

“Despite the recent complaints of killings and rustling of livestock, especially from eastern Jibia, relative calm has been restored in the area,” he said.

Ado said some repentant bandits had also begun assisting communities in protecting residents and maintaining peace.

He added that the process had facilitated the recovery and return of livestock and other valuables allegedly taken from residents.

Similar improvements have been reported in Batsari, Safana and Danmusa, although residents said the calm remained fragile and could easily collapse without sustained security measures.

Kankara renews peace deal as previous accord failed

The peace accord recently reached between communities in Kankara LGA and armed bandits has continued to generate mixed reactions, with residents reporting improved security while some bandit leaders have raised concerns over the arrest of their members.

Residents said the previous accord failed to restore security to communities, forcing community leaders to initiate a fresh deal.

The agreement, signed a few days ago, was described by the Chairman of the Kankara Local Government Security Committee, Sanusi Mohammed Nagoro, as one of the most successful peace initiatives in the state.

Nagoro said the process involved extensive consultations with community leaders, security agencies, elders and leaders of the bandit groups.

A community leader, Alhaji Bello Kankara, said the accord was reached under the supervision of Deputy Governor Faruk Lawal Jobe.

However, a bandit leader, Adamu Aliero, raised concerns over the arrest of some members of his group who returned from Saudi Arabia after participating in the 2026 Hajj.

In a video circulating on social media, Aliero alleged that the affected individuals were arrested at Katsina airport after returning from the pilgrimage.

He questioned why they were allowed to complete the processes for the Hajj only to be arrested on their return.

“If the government knew that these people would be arrested, why were they allowed to go through all the necessary processes and procedures to travel for Hajj in the first place, only to be arrested at the airport on their return?” he asked.

He warned that such actions could undermine trust in the peace process.

Meanwhile, a community leader who spoke to Daily Trust on condition of anonymity said Kankara had recorded about five consecutive days without an attack.

He said the development had also encouraged more people to attend the weekly Tuesday market in Kankara.

The Kankara council chairman, Alhaji Kasimu Dantsoho, did not respond to calls and messages seeking his reaction.

queue.title: FCTA begins demolition as encroachment spreads
queue.description: The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, yesterday directed the immediate demolition of houses and other structures obstructing designated water channels and green spaces across the capital. The exercise came barely three days after heavy rainfall submerged homes, businesses and vehicles in parts of the FCT, including the highbrow Maitama District. While […]
queue.content:
The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, yesterday directed the immediate demolition of houses and other structures obstructing designated water channels and green spaces across the capital.

The exercise came barely three days after heavy rainfall submerged homes, businesses and vehicles in parts of the FCT, including the highbrow Maitama District.

While the FCT Administration said the demolition was necessary to restore waterways and prevent further flooding, those whose businesses were affected alleged that they were caught off guard and left counting their losses.

Wike, who gave the directive after inspecting flood-affected areas in Maitama, said the demolition would commence immediately and continue until Saturday, irrespective of ongoing political activities or the status of the owners of the affected properties.

  • Police probe viral video of officers extorting motorists in Kaduna
  • 2027: Atiku absent as parties, candidates sign peace accord

 

“We will demolish all those houses found on the water channel. Some of them (the owners) are senators. Some of them are big men. Whether there is an election or no election, all those houses will go down. Heaven will not fall. Rather, heaven will be at peace that the right thing has been done,” he said.

The minister said the affected structures were not recently constructed and were largely owned by wealthy Nigerians, stressing that the government would no longer allow social status to prevent the enforcement of development regulations.

“In all those built-up areas that were not supposed to be built up, not a single poor person will live there. Those houses are houses built by well-to-do Nigerians. Those houses are not houses that were built last week. Those houses were there 10 years ago, eight years ago.

“I’m going to bring those houses down. Any house that is found on the water channel will go down. From today to Saturday, if Development Control delays, let them find any excuse to run away,” Wike warned.

The minister also frowned at the conversion of designated green areas in the capital into other uses, vowing that the administration would protect Abuja’s environmental assets.

He said the government would continue to enforce planning regulations irrespective of how long illegal developments had existed, adding that the administration would focus on addressing problems in the FCT rather than engage in political arguments.

Daily Trust had reported how several mansions, particularly at Goalview Estate, Maitama Extension, Abuja, were flooded over the weekend.

Residents attributed the incident partly to indiscriminate construction along waterways and the blockage of drainage channels in the area.

But findings by one of our correspondents yesterday showed that the flooding may have been worsened by the obstruction of a major canal in the area.

Residents told Daily Trust that the canal had been covered with concrete to create a platform for construction, allegedly for a building linked to a serving senator from the North-East.

A visit to the area on Tuesday showed that a section of the major canal had actually been covered with concrete, apparently to create space for the construction of a structure.

Residents said the development had narrowed the waterway and obstructed the free flow of water along the corridor.

They attributed the severity of Saturday’s flooding in the area, in part, to the obstruction of the canal, saying the waterway could no longer accommodate the volume of runoff generated by the heavy rainfall.

They also alleged that some structures in the area were being erected on portions previously designated as green areas or within corridors meant to serve as waterways.

Daily Trust also observed that the problem was not limited to Goalview Estate and its environs, as several locations within Maitama District previously designated as green areas or drainage corridors are now being demarcated and developed.

Such activities were particularly noticeable along both sides of Ibrahim Babangida Boulevard and Alvan Ikoku Way where portions of open spaces and areas that serve as natural drainage routes are undergoing construction.

The situation has raised questions about compliance with approved building plans, the protection of drainage corridors and the enforcement of development regulations in the nation’s capital.

Business owners, others in anguish

Business owners and workers affected by the demolition of structures in parts of Maitama, including Maitama Extension and the old WAEC building area around the Mississippi axis, have appealed to the FCT Administration to reconsider the exercise and provide a humane resolution.

They said they were caught off guard by the demolition, which they claimed had resulted in the loss of businesses, livelihoods and personal belongings.

Among those affected was the owner of Xpressor, Mustafa Onimisi, who described the exercise as inhumane.

Onimisi said the affected business owners had been informed by officials that their properties would be marked and that they would be given time to respond to the situation.

He said they were expecting an opportunity to engage with the authorities and find a solution before any demolition took place.

“We were told yesterday (Monday) by the director that they would mark them and give us two weeks. But to our great surprise, we woke up this morning and heard that the FCT minister was here himself and ordered the demolition,” he said.

He said though the FCTA has the authority to enforce its policies, the process should have been handled with greater consideration for those whose businesses and properties were affected.

“The minister is the alpha and omega, but he could have put a human face to the process. You are not dealing with fowls,” Onimisi said.

He appealed to the authorities to engage the affected business owners and consider a mutually acceptable solution.

“We should sit down and synergise and look at the best possible way forward. It is for the best interest of everyone around,” he said.

Onimisi, who identified himself as an indigene of Kogi State, said he was not the only person affected by the demolition, adding that several businesses in the area had suffered losses.

Workers at the affected businesses also expressed concern about the impact of the exercise on their livelihoods.

During a visit to the area, some affected persons were seen scrambling to retrieve their belongings from the structures as demolition work continued.

Some residents also pointed to an unfinished block of apartments whose owner was not immediately known, with the structure located close to the drainage channel.

 

More structures marked for demolition

Officials of the Federal Capital Development Authority (FCDA) also yesterday demolished the perimeter fence and part of a gym structure at a residential property on Mississippi Street, Maitama, Abuja.

The demolition reportedly affected parts of the property, including the perimeter fence, air-conditioning units and other items, according to one Yusufu Aminu, who said he was related to the owner of the property.

Aminu told Daily Trust that he was alerted by the property’s security personnel after officials arrived at the premises at about 8am with demolition control vehicles.

“They came on Monday and gave us a notice, you know, like a two-week notice for us to remove our items that are here, for the marked-out areas that we need to remove, which is fine. At least it is a two-week notice. Even if it is a one-week notice, at least we are there to comply.

“So, all of a sudden, they came today (yesterday), they said the FCT minister came, and now he instructed them to demolish this place, to demolish the fence. Let them give us time for us to move our items. They didn’t listen to us,” he said.

Aminu said the property had been affected by flooding for several years, which he attributed to a newer building allegedly constructed over a major canal close to the residence.

“We never had any issue with flooding, not until the building sprang up and we’ve been complaining. We’ve been to the development control on many occasions, telling them that our house is flooding as a result of this building.

“We’ve been experiencing flooding several times. Even our vehicle, our buildings, our house, they all got flooded. Our building, our vehicle got flooded as well. So, now, why has this very house that is sitting on the main canal, where the water is supposed to pass through, not been touched while you are on a cycle? That’s the question that we need to ask. Why is this building still sitting on the canal?”

Daily Trust could not independently verify the allegations concerning the approval of the structures, the alleged canal encroachment or the circumstances surrounding the demolition.

 

Experts worry over encroachment on green areas

Speaking to Daily Trust, a real estate expert, Bashir Musa, said there had been infractions on green areas in the last three years, particularly in highbrow districts such as Guzape, Maitama, the Central Business District (CBD), Katampe, Wuse and Kado.

In some instances, he said, specially designated areas were being converted into residential structures or used for other purposes, including the construction of business outlets.

He said: “The sad development is a disaster in waiting, considering that such areas are secured to preserve the natural setting of the capital city as a way of ensuring the safety of residents while also maintaining the beauty of the capital city.

“In Guzape, a green area located along Abdulrahman Okene Street, where a U-shaped land totalling 3.4 hectares was originally allocated as a park and recreational area, has been used for residential buildings.

“Also, in the Central Business District (CBD), a number of places that have been reserved for conservation, parks and water channels, among others, have been converted to other purposes.

“I have personally seen another area that has been reassigned from a green area to a residential area behind Government Secondary School, Area 3, Garki. Already, plots are being fenced ahead of construction. The new plots could be seen from the NNPC mega station.”

Musa said the situation would turn Abuja into a flooding zone if nothing was done immediately.

Another expert, Bldr Joy Bolaji, described the recent flooding as a product of bad urban planning that must be corrected, while identifying some flood hotspots.

“If you look around FCT now, you will see that construction work is going on in green areas. For instance, there is one ongoing on a green area and floodplain around the National Mosque. The site is crammed on both sides of the Nigeria-Export Import Bank, City Park and the Wood Bridge Park.

“Also, there was a very popular park and garden in Wuse Zone 6 opposite Sky Memorial junction; that place is now almost fully developed for commercial purposes, and as an expert I feel sad seeing all these things,” he said.

Bolaji stressed that something must be done immediately to avert a crisis that “may be difficult to contend with”

Also, the past chairperson of the Nigerian Institute of Town Planners, FCT chapter, Lami Ayuba, said the craving by influential people to live in some popular districts like Maitama, Guzape and Garki was putting pressure on government officials to convert green areas to residential buildings.

She said the pressure from various quarters was making some officials violate the master plan by re-allocating green areas for other purposes or mixed use, as the case may be.

She said that “unless something urgent was done, the annual disaster at the Trademore Estate, Lugbe District, would be witnessed in other districts.”

 

‘Wike’s demolition order coming too late’

Speaking on Wike’s directive on the demolition of structures built on waterways and other environmentally sensitive areas, a town planning expert and former Coordinator of the Abuja Metropolitan Management Council (AMMC), Umar Shuaibu, described the action as coming too late to prevent the flooding already confronting Abuja.

Shuaibu, a town planning expert, said the government ought to have acted months earlier when warnings were issued about the likelihood of severe weather conditions and the need to keep waterways and drainage channels clear.

He said waiting until flooding had begun before ordering the removal of illegal structures amounted to a reactive rather than preventive approach to urban planning.

According to him, the National Meteorological Agency (NiMet) had raised concerns around February and March about the expected weather conditions, giving authorities sufficient time to clear drainage channels and prevent further encroachment on waterways.

“Since around February and March, NiMet predicted that there are so many areas in this country that this year’s weather is going to be devastating.

“So all authorities should make sure they clear drains. They should make sure they don’t develop where it is a water path,” he said.

Shuaibu said the flooding being witnessed in parts of Abuja should not be viewed merely as a natural disaster, arguing that the problem had been aggravated by human activities, particularly the conversion of green areas, waterways and drainage corridors to building sites.

He identified several locations where he alleged that development had taken place in areas originally designated as green zones or water channels.

He cited the Zone 6 neighbourhood in Wuse, where he said a major sewer line traversed a green area but had been removed to pave the way for construction.

“Take an example of Zone 6 neighbourhood in Wuse. That area, apart from being a green area, there is a major sewer line that traverses that land. It is now removed. Construction is going on there,” he said.

The former AMMC coordinator also mentioned the area around the Villa Gate, where he said a green park located close to the entrance had been built over.

“The green park is by the left before the gate. Extensive green park. And there are service lines under that one also. It’s now also built,” he said.

He further identified a large expanse of land between Halley Brothers and the Mega Filling Station in the Central Area as another area where development had encroached on a natural water channel.

According to him, the area, known as the Wupa water basin, was previously left undeveloped because of its role as a natural water channel.

“To your left, if you are coming from Wuse to the Central Area, you see a very vast land. Before, it was fully green because it’s a water channel. We call that Wupa water basin.

“So that area has been completely cleared, ready for construction,” he said.

Shuaibu warned that tampering with natural waterways could have serious consequences because water would eventually find another route whenever its original passage was blocked.

He cited the situation around the Central Area, where, according to him, a wide natural stream had been narrowed to only a few culverts.

He said the channel had been designed with a buffer zone within which no development was supposed to take place, but that the natural watercourse had nevertheless been altered.

“When the first rain came, it overflowed the culvert because the two or three channels that are there will not convey the water that is coming from the upper level. So it created its own path, a very big gully by the side.

“Because water most definitely takes its own way,” he said.

The town planner said the resulting environmental degradation was a direct consequence of such violations, stressing that retaining the natural water channels would have helped reduce the impact of flooding.

“There is complete environmental degradation in that area now. What we are seeing now is a consequence of some of those violations,” he said.

Shuaibu also criticised the FCT administration for focusing on demolition without addressing how the structures were allowed to emerge in the first place.

He questioned the authorities responsible for allocating the lands and approving developments in areas where construction should not have been permitted.

He argued that officials who knowingly allocated or approved developments on green areas and waterways should also be held accountable.

“If he (Wike) didn’t order the allocation, he must discipline the people who allocated the land there and bring them to book,” he said.

The town planner said merely deploying bulldozers to demolish a few structures would amount to a cosmetic response if the government failed to revoke illegal allocations and sanction those responsible for granting them.

“The way forward is removing all those developments that are unauthorised. All those developments, all those plots that have been allocated in green areas, must be revoked,” he said.

Shuaibu further urged the FCT administration not to spare influential property owners whose buildings may have been constructed on waterways or other prohibited areas.

He maintained that the current flooding challenge should serve as a wake-up call for the government to return to strict enforcement of Abuja’s master plan and prevent further encroachment on waterways, drainage corridors and green areas.

He said the authorities should conduct a comprehensive review of land allocations and building approvals in environmentally sensitive locations, revoke illegal allocations and prosecute officials and individuals found to have violated planning regulations.

 

By Vincent A. Yusuf,  Itodo Daniel Sule, Dalhatu Liman, Habeebat Ajayi & Philip Shimnom Clement

queue.title: TETFund: Lighting Up Nigeria, Projecting a Culture of Excellence Across Africa and the World
queue.description: By Eniola Olakunri “Nigeria must begin to reflect excellence, discipline, and integrity in all aspects of national life….the era of dilapidated public facilities must give way to infrastructure that mirrors
queue.content:
By Eniola Olakunri

“Nigeria must begin to reflect excellence, discipline, and integrity in all aspects of national life….the era of dilapidated public facilities must give way to infrastructure that mirrors the dignity of the Nigerian people.”

— Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, President and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, Federal Republic of Nigeria

It is no gainsaying that the Tertiary Education Trust Fund (TETFund) is kinetically transforming Nigeria’s public tertiary education landscape and contributing significantly to the enormous national machinery being deployed to accelerate the country’s socio-economic development.

Indeed, TETFund’s evolving story is increasingly becoming one of vision, intervention, innovation and excellence – an institutional success story that is beginning to resonate well beyond Nigeria’s borders.

There is an instructive lesson from the remarkable transformation of Dubai.

In his book, My Vision: Challenges in the Race for Excellence, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Ruler of Dubai and Prime Minister and Vice President of the United Arab Emirates, observed that at a certain stage in Dubai’s development, the emirate essentially stopped competing with others and began competing with itself.

That mindset was pivotal.

Having moved ahead of many of its regional peers, Dubai’s challenge was no longer simply to catch up with anyone else, but to continuously surpass its own achievements. Its remarkable transformation subsequently became a source of inspiration for other countries in the region.

The ripple effect is evident across the Middle East. Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman, among others, have unveiled ambitious development visions designed to diversify their economies, invest in human capital, accelerate innovation and reduce dependence on traditional sources of revenue.

Saudi Arabia’s futuristic NEOM project, Qatar’s aggressive investment strategy, Bahrain’s Vision 2030, Kuwait’s Vision 2035 and Oman’s Vision 2040 all speak to a region increasingly determined to compete not merely with others, but with the limitations of its own past.

Therein lies an important lesson for Nigeria – and, indeed, for TETFund.

TETFund, established by Nigerian law to provide intervention and support for the development of tertiary education, appears to have entered a phase where it is not merely fulfilling its statutory mandate but increasingly competing with its own records of achievement.

The Fund is progressively raising the bar on what is possible in Nigeria’s public tertiary institutions, intervening in infrastructure, research, innovation, academic staff development, teaching and learning facilities and other areas critical to restoring and sustaining standards.

Its reach extends beyond conventional universities, polytechnics and colleges of education and include top-tier educational institutions operated by the nation’s security agencies – the Army, Navy, Air Force and Police.

The significance of this should not be underestimated.

For decades, the conversation around public education in Nigeria was dominated by the challenges of decaying infrastructure, inadequate facilities, insufficient research capacity and the persistent erosion of standards.

TETFund has emerged as one of the principal instruments through which government is confronting these challenges.

More importantly, however, Nigeria may now be exporting an education intervention model that other African countries consider worthy of emulation.

From Nigeria to The Gambia and Beyond

A compelling indication of this emerging influence came recently when The Gambia announced its intention to understudy the TETFund model.

The Gambian Minister of Higher Education, Research, Science and Technology, Hon. Prof. Pierre Gomez, led a high-powered delegation to TETFund’s headquarters in Maitama, Abuja, where they were received by the management team led by the Executive Secretary, Arc. (Dr.) Sonny S.T. Echono.

Prof. Gomez disclosed that The Gambia had established its own Tertiary and Higher Education Trust Fund (THET), modelled substantially on Nigeria’s TETFund experience.

The delegation therefore sought TETFund’s cooperation and support in opening its institutional doors and sharing its experience with officials of THET, who are expected to undertake a study tour of the Fund’s operations.

According to the Gambian delegation, the country had consistently followed TETFund’s activities through its website, social media platforms and other communication channels and had become convinced that establishing a similar intervention mechanism would provide an added fillip to the Gambian government’s efforts to transform its tertiary education sector.

The proposed collaboration is expected to encompass areas such as research and capacity development and, importantly, strengthen the already existing diplomatic relationship between Nigeria and The Gambia.

That is a significant endorsement.

It means that an institution created primarily to address Nigeria’s own tertiary education challenges is now attracting attention as a reference point for education-sector intervention elsewhere in Africa.

And The Gambia is not alone.

Tanzania’s Education Authority (TEA), Ghana’s Education Trust Fund (GETFund) and Sierra Leone’s Tertiary Education Commission (TEC) are among institutions whose mandates and activities reflect similar efforts to strengthen tertiary education through structured intervention and funding mechanisms.

Nigeria, through TETFund, is therefore increasingly participating in a broader African conversation about how to sustainably finance, modernise and reposition higher education for the demands of the 21st century.

From Infrastructure to Innovation

TETFund’s mandate is broad and consequential.

It encompasses essential physical infrastructure for teaching and learning, instructional materials and equipment, research and publication, academic staff training and development, as well as other areas considered critical to improving and maintaining standards in higher education.

Over the years, the Fund has continued to deepen its intervention across Nigerian tertiary institutions.

And the next frontier appears increasingly to be research, innovation and the commercialisation of knowledge.

In a bold move to unlock Nigeria’s vast human and natural resources, stimulate innovation and accelerate socio-economic transformation, TETFund recently approved N7.5 billion for 174 cutting-edge research projects under the 2025 National Research Fund (NRF) Grant Cycle.

That intervention represents more than a financial commitment.

It is a recognition that Nigeria cannot educate its way into prosperity merely by producing graduates. The country must also produce ideas, technologies, intellectual property, solutions and enterprises capable of solving its most pressing developmental challenges.

The Fund’s support for research into vaccines for diseases such as COVID-19 and Lassa fever further demonstrates the potential of tertiary institutions to become engines of national problem-solving rather than simply centres for the transmission of knowledge.

Similarly, the provision of substantial innovation funding to university students signals a shift from the traditional model in which students are expected merely to graduate and search for employment.

The emerging model is one in which young Nigerians can be encouraged and supported to become creators, innovators, employers and entrepreneurs – even before leaving university.

That is precisely the kind of thinking required to build a knowledge economy.

The National Research Fair

TETFund’s planned second National Research Fair, expected in November, provides another important platform for this emerging ecosystem.

The Fair offers an opportunity to identify, showcase and support innovative ideas from across the country, regardless of the social or economic background of their originators, provided they successfully navigate the established expert evaluation process.

Such platforms matter because many potentially transformative Nigerian ideas never progress beyond laboratories, lecture rooms, notebooks and prototypes.

The challenge is to create pathways through which research can move from idea to prototype, prototype to product, and product to enterprise.

A properly structured research and innovation ecosystem can strengthen Nigeria’s knowledge economy, improve industrial competitiveness, create employment and provide practical solutions to some of the country’s most urgent developmental problems.

Excellence Has No Finish Line

For the Board and Management of TETFund, excellence appears to have no finish line.

The Fund seems increasingly determined to challenge itself at every turn – to exceed previous accomplishments, close the door against institutional complacency and demonstrate that what was once considered impossible can become achievable through vision, discipline, resources and purposeful execution.

Its ultimate ambition should therefore be viewed beyond the immediate construction of buildings or provision of equipment.

The bigger opportunity is to help transform Nigeria into a global powerhouse in knowledge, research, innovation, science, technology and human capital development.

And there is a sense of urgency about this.

Nigeria cannot afford to wait indefinitely.

The country possesses an enormous reservoir of youthful talent, intellectual capacity, natural resources and entrepreneurial energy. What is required is the institutional architecture to convert these assets into sustainable national prosperity.

TETFund is one of the institutions positioned to play a defining role in that transformation.

Its growing impact is therefore not simply about the number of projects commissioned, buildings constructed, researchers supported or institutions reached.

It is ultimately about changing the possibilities available to the Nigerian student, researcher, academic and innovator.

Nigeria’s Opportunity to Lead

TETFund may well have started as an intervention agency designed to rescue Nigeria’s tertiary institutions from years of infrastructural and developmental neglect.

But the trajectory today suggests something considerably bigger.

The Fund is increasingly demonstrating that a Nigerian public institution can build systems, break its own records, institutionalise excellence and become a reference point for others.

The emerging interest from African countries is particularly instructive.

If The Gambia is looking towards Nigeria for lessons; if other African education institutions are studying similar intervention models; and if Nigeria is beginning to export not just people and culture but also institutional solutions, then TETFund has entered a new phase of relevance.

This is perhaps one of the most compelling dimensions of the Fund’s evolution.

Nigeria has for too long been accustomed to importing models, ideas and institutional frameworks from abroad.

There is absolutely nothing wrong with learning from successful countries.

But there comes a point when a nation must also begin to develop solutions worthy of emulation by others.

TETFund appears to be approaching that point.

With the support of its Board of Trustees under the leadership of the Right Honourable Aminu Bello Masari and the focused management team led by Arc. (Dr.) Sonny S.T. Echono, the Fund has an opportunity to deepen this trajectory and establish itself not merely as Nigeria’s foremost tertiary education intervention agency, but as an African reference institution in education financing, research intervention and human-capital development.

The challenge now is to sustain the momentum, institutionalise the gains and ensure that excellence becomes not an occasional achievement but a permanent culture.

For TETFund, the race is no longer simply to catch up.

The race is to continuously outdo itself.

And if it succeeds in doing so, Nigeria will not merely be lighting up its tertiary education system.

It will be lighting up Africa – and projecting a distinctly Nigerian culture of excellence to the world.

*Eniola Olakunri , Public Sector Analyst and CEO, Write Affairs, writes from Abuja.

queue.title: Crisis Rocks NDC Over Alleged Replacement of N’Assembly Candidate in Rivers
queue.description: Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja A fresh crisis is rocking the Nigerian Democratic Congress (NDC) following the alleged replacement of the House of Representatives candidate on the Independent National Electoral Commission
queue.content:
Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja

A fresh crisis is rocking the Nigerian Democratic Congress (NDC) following the alleged replacement of the House of Representatives candidate on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) portal.

Recall that the National Election Committee led by Dr. Osusu Osusu had on 29 May 2026 conducted a direct primary to elect the House of Representatives candidate for Port Harcourt Federal Constituency 1.

The electoral committee publicly declared Prince Abele Wobo winner with 292 votes.

However, a group, the Social Accountability Forum in a statement issued Sunday and jointly signed by its Coordinator, Elechi Kingsley, and Secretary, Godspower Nyebuchi said despite the declaration, the name of Hon. Manuchim Umezurike, the current member representing the Constituency, was uploaded on the INEC portal in place of Prince Wobo.

The group noted: “Prince Abele Wobo lawfully emerged as the candidate of the NDC for Port Harcourt Constituency 1. The result was announced publicly by the Chairman of the National Electoral Committee, Dr. Osusu Osusu.”

The group alleged that Hon. Umezurike did not participate in the primary as he was still a member of the All Progressives Congress (APC) at the time.

“Having been denied a return ticket by the APC, some people in the NDC are now in connivance to legitimize an illegality. They are trying to forge documents to support the substitution since the matter is already in court,” the group stated.

The group claimed that pressure was mounted on Dr. Osusu to recant the result and issue a new one in favour of the substituted candidate, but he allegedly refused.

“They are now trying to discredit and disclaim the entire primary conducted by Dr. Osusu Osusu because he refused to compromise his integrity.” 

The group described the development as a direct assault on internal democracy,  warning that it could destroy public trust in the party ahead of 2027.

It called on the NDC national leadership to immediately correct the anomaly and restore Wobo’s name on the portal to preserve the integrity of the party and electoral process.

The group added: “It is undemocratic and dangerous to conduct an open primary, declare a winner, and then substitute him in the dead of night. That is the definition of impunity.” 

it noted that the matter has been taken to court, with Umezurike reportedly served through substituted means.

queue.title: ADVERTISEMENT INVITATION FOR EXPRESSION OF INTEREST (EOI) FOR THE RECRUITMENT OF STAFF OF VALUE CHAIN PROGRAMME IN NORTHERN NIGERIA (VCN)
queue.description: Background The Value Chain for Northern Nigeria (VCN) Programme is a flagship initiative of the Federal Government of Nigeria, implemented through the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security (FMAFS) in partnership with the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) and the French Development Agency (AFD). The overall development objective of VCN is to increase […]
queue.content:
Background

The Value Chain for Northern Nigeria (VCN) Programme is a flagship initiative of the Federal Government of Nigeria, implemented through the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security (FMAFS) in partnership with the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) and the French Development Agency (AFD). The overall development objective of VCN is to increase incomes, food security, and resilience of smallholder farmers and other value chain actors in Northern Nigeria through competitive, climate‑resilient, and inclusive agricultural value chains. Specifically, the Programme aims to transform priority agricultural value chains in Northern Nigeria to drive food security, employment, and inclusive economic growth, with a strong focus on women, youth, and vulnerable groups.

The Programme is financed through multiple financing sources, including IFAD and AFD loans and will run until 31 March 2034 (financial closure: 30 September 2034). Implementation of the programme will be based on a decentralised approach through federal and state programme implementation units under the coordination of the Federal Department of Development Partners Projects (FD‑DPP). The National Programme Coordinating Office (NPCO) will be based in Abuja, and the State Programme Implementation Unit (SPIU) in each participating state. The participating states are: Sokoto, Kebbi, Jigawa, Zamfara, Borno, Katsina, Yobe, Bauchi and Kano.

The NPMU will be staffed by a multidisciplinary team, including: National Programme Coordinator, Monitoring & Evaluation Specialist, Agricultural Production and Rural Infrastructure Specialists, Rural Institutions Development Specialist, Knowledge Management and Communication Specialist, Food & Nutrition Specialist, ICT4D Support Specialist, Gender & Social Inclusion and GALS Specialists, Climate & Environment Specialist, Financial Controller, Accountant, Finance Officer, Senior Internal Auditor, Procurement Specialist and Officers, and National administrative and HR support staff. State Programme Implementation Unit will mirror these functions (with a few exceptions) at the state level, ensuring strong fiduciary oversight, timely reporting from SPIU, and harmonized accounting procedures resulting in an effective last‑mile delivery.

Governance and accountability will be anchored in a National Steering Committee, supported by technical committees as required, to provide policy guidance, ensure alignment with national priorities, and resolve strategic bottlenecks. The implementation of the project will include high-risk operating environments, hence project staff/specialists at both National and State levels must possess the skills and expertise to work in fragile areas, demonstrating a high level of sensitivity to conflict and crisis situations. Additionally, prior experience of project staff/specialist in remote project monitoring and implementation using dedicated tools to effectively track project activities would be crucial.

Qualified and experienced officers are required to fill the following positions in the VCN National Programme Coordination Office (NPCO) to serve as;

  1. National Programme Coordinator (NPC),
  2. Monitoring and Evaluation Specialist (MES)
  • Agricultural Production Specialist (APS)
  1. Rural Infrastructure Engineer Specialist (RIS)
  2. Food and Nutrition Specialist (FNS)
  3. ICT4D Support Specialist (ICT4D)
  • Gender Inclusion/Social Safeguards Specialist (GSIS)
  • Rural Institutions Development Specialist (RIDS)
  1. Climate Change and Environment Safeguards Specialist (CES)
  2. Knowledge Management and Communication Specialist
  3. Financial Controller (FC)
  • Accountant
  • Finance Officer
  • Senior Internal Auditor
  1. Procurement Specialist
  • Procurement Officer
  • Procurement Assistant
  • National Administrative and Human Resource Officer

Position And Specific Requirements for Expression Of Interest (EOI)

Key Position 1: National Programme Coordinator (NPC)

  1. Position Overview

Under the direct supervision of the Director of the Federal Department of Development Partners Projects (FD-DPP) of the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security (FMAFS), the NPC will be responsible for the overall management and implementation of the VCN. She/he will also be responsible for managing the team of specialists within the NPCO and ensuring their performance, as well as that of the service providers hired to implement programme activities. A key element of the position will be to ensure that the programme achieves its development objectives. The National Programme Coordinator will have responsibilities for activities of the nine (9) State Programme Offices. Coordinators of each of the state offices will report directly to the National Coordinator and will also be involved in the activities of the States as appropriate.

2. Key Responsibilities

A. Early Implementation Tasks

  1. Oversee the establishment of the NPCO, and the recruitment and deployment of NPCO staff
  2. Oversee the establishment and functioning of State Programme Coordination Offices (SPCOs), the recruitment of staff for as well as the establishment of their offices and equipping with initial essential equipment
  • Facilitate the formation of the Programme Steering Committee (PSC).
  1. Serve as leader of the programme management team in order to achieve the following responsibilities: (i) Programme Implementation Coordination; (ii) Financial/Asset Management; (iii) Contract Management; (iv) Personnel Management (v) Government Liaison/External Relations; and (vi) Knowledge Management and Policy Development.
  2. Ensure the M&E system for the Programme is developed and implemented in a timely manner that represents the needs of key stakeholders.
  3. Lead the completion and regular reviews of the Programme Implementation Manual (PIM), and other guidelines;
  • Guide the establishment of administrative, accounting and programme-outcome and M&E systems;
  • In collaboration with FMAFS, coordinate training workshops on the programme strategy and approaches, AWPB and procurement for the first year with key stakeholders to ensure an updated and shared understanding of the programme strategy and information needs;
  1. Ensure that an effective and participatory M&E system is established and effective.
  2. Ensure the Programme is annually audited by the Internal Audit Unit of FMFAS as well as an approved External Auditor by IFAD and

B. Programme Management

  1. Head the secretariat of the National Steering Committee (NSC) at meetings related to VCN.
  2. Coordinate the implementation of VCN among the participating states.
  • Provide guidance to the Program staff at both the national and state levels.
  1. Collaborate with and support the Country Programme Advisory Team (CPAT).
  2. Liaise with other relevant programmes and technical departments in the public sector and private Sector.
  3. Consolidate the states’ Annual Work Plan and Budget (AWPB) along with that of the NPCO and submit it in a timely manner to the Lead Agency and IFAD for approval.
  • Oversee the contracting of support staff, consultants, and service providers.
  • Convene and host periodic meetings with the NPCO staff and key staff of the SPIU
  1. Ensure timely delivery of quality reports (AWPB, semi-annual reports, financial statements, audit reports, M&E reports, etc.) to FMAFS, IFAD, and AFD.
  2. Coordinate supervision missions and ensure the implementation of recommendations (supervision and audits).
  3. Organize impact evaluation, beneficiary assessment, Mid-Term Review, and Final Evaluation of VCN.
  • Present the AWPB and M&E plan to the relevant approval bodies (the PSC and IFAD, AFD and/or DP) in a timely manner for review and approval; and on the basis of the AWPB, authorise the subsequent release of funds.
  • For each service provider contract, ensure that detailed specifications are prepared in a timely, objective, fair and transparent manner, including the M&E responsibilities and administration of terms and awards.
  • Ensure the holistic implementation of the programme, ensuring the programme outcomes and levels are seamlessly joined in the pursuit of market-led poverty alleviation amongst poor rural households
  1. Make sure the business of the programme is conducted in an efficient manner by supervising and monitoring programme implementation. Ensure that timely decisions on corrective actions are made and implemented
  • Direct and supervise the day-to-day operations of the programme, guided by the PDR, PIM and the AWPB, providing any necessary amendments to ensure smooth performance.
  • Mobilize relevant technical assistance in a timely manner, with clearly demarcated responsibilities that are based on the participatory and equity principles of the programme
  • Assure that all contractual obligations are adhered to and make the necessary contacts and efforts to ensure implementation meets programme targets
  • Regularly appraise staff and provide feedback and support to enable them to do their jobs.
  1. Check the monthly Programme financial report for accuracy and appropriateness. Regularly meet with the Financial Controller concerning financial reporting issues, errors, trends, payment delays and related matters.
  • Develop close working relationships with all programme participants and stakeholders – including the primary stakeholders, FMFAS, FMF and other Government agencies, private sector and NGOs – all parties required to establish a shared vision of the programme to achieve objectives.
  • Establish and maintain good working relations with the relevant government ministries, as well as other higher-level stakeholder groups
  • Coordinate the activities of Implementing Partners (IPs) and in particular FMFAS/State Ministries for Agriculture and Food Security, NGOs and Technical Service Providers (TSPs) to ensure effective delivery of Programme services.
  • Promote collaboration with IFAD, AFD and other Development Partners (DPs), and the private sector on value chain development.
  • Take full responsibility for procurement of goods and services in programme implementation. Approve contracts for all transactions undertaken by the Programme after obtaining all the necessary no-objections.
  • Ensure timely and appropriate reporting on progress and problems of Programme implementation, including Quarterly and Annual Operational and Financial Progress Reports on the Project’s activities.
  • Ensure easy public access to M&E reports and data and make sure they are widely distributed.
  • Submit required analytical reports on progress – including indications of planned actions and financial statements – on time and to the relevant bodies, with assistance from M&E staff.
  • Encourage staff to report frankly on fieldwork, highlighting problems and possible solutions plus lessons learned. Reward innovation in critical reflection and learning
  • Ensure the planning of and participation in key reflection moments – in particular, the annual programme reviews.
  • Sign implementation agreements with the implementing partners, defining the modalities for implementation and M&E. Ensure that participatory M&E and learning initiatives are specified in terms consistent with the direction of the programme.
  • Make all efforts to engage key stakeholders in important external evaluations to ensure an understanding of locally perceived impacts and problems.
  • See that all ad hoc evaluation studies needed to gain timely and relevant insights into emerging areas of concern are undertaken. Make sure the resulting data is shared with all those involved in decision-making and follow up on the implementation of any decisions
  • Support external missions in ways that foster a joint learning process that identifies how the programme could be improved further to achieve impact.
  • Ensure that mission recommendations are followed up and executed as intended to achieve maximum impact of project objectives.
  • Undertake any other responsibility that will ensure smooth and effective implementation of the Programme.

3. Required Qualifications and Experience

Academic Education

At least a master’s or higher-level University degree in Agriculture, Agricultural Economics, or other relevant discipline.

Professional Certification

Active membership in a recognized professional project management, management, or agricultural body (PMP, CMI, NIM, NIPM, CIPM, or equivalent) is an added advantage.

Professional Experience

  • Minimum Ten (10) years relevant working experience, of which seven (7) years’ experience is in project management or agriculture-related management positions of internationally funded agricultural development projects, preferably with IFAD, World Bank, AfDB, or similar multilateral development organizations.
  • Experience in Government and IFAD/AFD policies and procedures or donor-funded policies and procedures, including agriculture, nutrition, gender, climate change and environment, and general programme finance and administration.
  • Proven record in the field of project preparation, coordination and supervision of agricultural projects, particularly agricultural Value Chains.
  • Possess high managerial experience and knowledge of strategic planning approaches.
  • Staff management experience including recruitment, appraisals, and managing performance.
  • Strong partnership-building skills from both the private and the public sector
  • Strong analytical and market-oriented skills
  • Computer Literacy: Possesses very good computer literacy in Office (Word, Excel, and PowerPoint), Email Clients (Microsoft Outlook), Video Conferencing (Zoom, Microsoft Teams), and Web Applications.

 

Personal Competencies

  • Management: Strong management skills, particularly the ability to provide strategic direction and technical supervision,
  • Results-driven leadership: Ability to drive results in a time-constrained environment with multiple competing priorities.
  • Problem-solving orientation: Proactive approach to identifying and resolving issues systematically.
  • Excellent communication: Ability to convey complex financial information clearly to non-financial stakeholders and to engage constructively with government counterparts.
  • Integrity and independence: Commitment to fiduciary standards with the ability to maintain professional independence.
  • Team builder: Capacity to mentor staff, standardize practices across dispersed teams, and foster accountability.
  • Reliable and responsible personality and capacity to work under demanding professional circumstances and in an international environment;
  • Excellent coordination and negotiation skills;
  • Language Skills. Fluency in written and spoken English and local Northern Nigerian languages.

4. Terms and Conditions

  • Contract Duration: The duration of the assignment will be a two-year staff contract with annual evaluation of performance in line with the respective job description in accordance with the recommendation of the FMAFS and renewable depending on satisfactory performance.
  • Travels: Regular travel to State PCOs in Sokoto, Kebbi, Jigawa, Zamfara, Borno, Katsina, Yobe, Bauchi and Kano. Occasional travel for IFAD / AFD missions and training.
  • Remuneration: Competitive package commensurate with qualifications and experience, in accordance with FGN/IFAD/AFD salary scales for nationally recruited project staff.

5. Undertaking

This is a full-time position, and the Project Coordinator for this assignment must not be engaged in any other on-going assignment in Nigeria or elsewhere at the time the employment contract comes into force. Non-compliance would lead to cancellation of the contract by the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security. Falsifying personal data will also lead to disqualification. The Project Coordinator should not have a current business relationship with potential FBOs or any other project partner.

6. Reporting and Location

  • Located in Abuja, the FCT, and will report directly to the Director, FDDPP of FMAFS.

 

 Key Position 2: Monitoring & Evaluation Specialist (MES)

1. Position Overview

Main responsibility and reporting lines: Under the direct supervision of the National Programme Coordinator (NPC), the MES will be in charge of all VCN M&E activities, including overseeing the State and LGA levels. The MES will also be responsible for compiling, validating and reporting M&E results and progress through collaboration with SPIUs and other Implementing Partners, and for the timely submission of reports.

2. Key Responsibilities

Develop a Project-Specific M&E Plan that will clearly detail: (i) description of the VCN M&E approach; (ii) VCN processes and activities to be implemented; (iii) the tools to be used for data collection and processing; (iii) the deliverables to be produced; and(iv) M&E responsibilities of all project teams to ensure smooth collaboration.

  1. Support the MIS Developer in the development of the VCN M&E MIS to ensure that data collection, beneficiary database, and reporting templates are consistent with the project M&E plan;
  2. Prepare and consolidate, in collaboration with the Finance Unit and technical specialists, the annual work plan and budget (AWPB);
  • Coordinate with State teams and implementation partners to collect and report data on project activities using the MIS as per the appropriate project data collection tools that are outlined in the M&E Plan;
  1. Experience in remote project monitoring using dedicated tools to effectively track project activities.
  2. Provide technical support to the project, State staff, and partners on M&E and MIS-related issues, including data collection, analysis, and reporting;
  3. Submit a timely updated Project Logframe and Physical progress performance and submit to IFAD before annual supervision missions;
  • Ensure the quality of data collected and reported by conducting quality assurance checks and providing feedback to project staff and partners;
  • Guide the service providers contracted to conduct the COI survey by ensuring the survey methodology and questionnaire adhere to the IFAD COIs.
  1. Ensure compliance with IFAD and Project requirements and ethical considerations related to data collection and use;
  2. Provide capacity to VCN, LGA, and State staff and partners on M&E and MIS-related issues, including data collection, analysis, and reporting;
  3. Manage project information, particularly the beneficiary database, documentation, and other project-related information;
  • Collaborate with the VCN KMC Specialist by providing evidence-based data on the impact of project interventions to guide the development of KMC products.
  • Carry out any other assignment or relevant duties in the field of his/her competencies as may be assigned by the Project Coordinator and/or other Authorities.
  • Perform other duties as directed by the NPC.

3. Key Outputs

  • Elaborated VCN contextual Project Specific M&E Plan by project start-up
  • Fully operational M&E Management Information System by project year 1
  • Fully developed data collection tools by project start-up
  • AWPB
  • Quarterly data analysis reports to inform implementation
  • Quarterly monitoring reports to support decision-making
  • Technical assistance to project and implementation partners
  • Capacity building materials (training materials, guidelines, toolkits) to build the capacity of project and implementation partners on M&E-related issues
  • Management of the beneficiaries’ database to ensure outreach is up to date, and reporting avoids double-counting

4. Required Qualifications and Experience

Academic Education

At least a master’s or higher-level university degree in statistics, demographics, public policy, international development, economics, or a related field. An advanced certificate in M&E, statistics, or economics is preferred.

Professional Certification

Active membership in a recognized professional project management, management, or agricultural body (PMP, PRINCE2, or equivalent) is an added advantage.

 

Professional Experience

  • Minimum of ten (10) years of relevant professional experience including seven (7) years in a similar role responsible for implementing M&E activities in internationally funded agricultural development projects, preferably with IFAD, World Bank, AfDB, or similar multilateral development organizations.
  • Experience in designing, implementing, and operating project M&E systems and plans from project initiation to closeout stages.
  • Experience in designing and managing beneficiary monitoring and database systems.
  • Experience in managing project-level M&E Management Information Systems (MIS).
  • Knowledge of the major evaluation methodologies (e.g., qualitative, quantitative, mixed-method, and impact) and data collection and analysis methodologies.
  • Experience in developing and refining data collection tools.
  • Experience with data quality assessments and oversight.
  • Extensive knowledge of IFAD COI guidelines and policies is an advantage.
  • Fluency in written and spoken English and local Northern Nigerian languages.

 

Technical Skills

  • Technical expertise: Possess a strong understanding of M&E concepts, methods, and tools. This includes the ability to design and implement M&E plans, develop data collection tools, and analyze data.
  • Communication Skills: Excellent communication skills to effectively communicate project progress, results, and recommendations to stakeholders such as donors, governments, and other key partners, and project staff;
  • Analytical Skills: Strong analytical skills to analyze data and identify trends, patterns, and areas of improvement. This includes the ability to use statistical software and other analytical tools to analyze data.
  • Project Management skills: Strong project management skills to effectively manage M&E activities, including developing plans, coordinating data collection, and ensuring timely reporting;
  • Teamwork and collaboration: Ability to work closely with project staff, implementing partners, and stakeholders to ensure that M&E activities are integrated into VCN implementation;
  • Problem-solving skills: Proven ability to identify issues and challenges related to M&E and to develop solutions to address them;
  • Ethical and professional conduct: Demonstrate ethical and professional standards in all aspects of work, including data collection, analysis, and reporting. This includes maintaining confidentiality and respecting the rights of beneficiaries.
  • Computer Literacy: Possesses very good computer literacy in Office (Word, Excel, and PowerPoint), Email Clients (Microsoft Outlook), Video Conferencing (Zoom, Microsoft Teams), and Web Applications.

 

Personal Competencies

  • Results-driven leadership: Ability to drive results in a time-constrained environment with multiple competing priorities.
  • Problem-solving orientation: Proactive approach to identifying and resolving issues systematically.
  • Excellent communication: Ability to convey complex M&E information clearly to all stakeholders and to engage constructively with government counterparts.
  • Integrity and independence: Commitment to fiduciary standards with the ability to maintain professional independence.
